I am 65 years old, and I have worked these 4.5 mu in Quzhou for 45 years. My wife and I are the only two in our household, so we keep things simple and grow what we know best: cotton. I never went to school, but I have learned more from this soil than any book could teach me.

It is spring, and the soil is warming up. I will till all 4.5 mu with my rotary tiller to break up the winter-hardened ground and bury the leftover stalks. I plant improved cotton seeds — the kind the seed station sells that resist bollworm — because they save me money on sprays and still produce the fluffy white bolls the buyers want. Before sowing, I will spread my fertilizer: nitrogen to push the leafy growth early on, phosphorus so the roots grow deep and can drink from the well, and potassium to fill the bolls out proper. I do not use a scale; I fertilize by feel and by the sack-load, but after all these years I know it works out to about 18 kg of nitrogen, 6 kg of phosphorus, and 10 kg of potassium on each mu.

I will irrigate three times from my well this season: once right after sowing to settle the seeds, once when the plants are flowering heavy in the summer heat, and once when the bolls are filling. Cotton can stand dry spells better than most crops, but those three waterings are what separate a bad year from a good one. I will spray pesticide four times — early for aphids, then to keep worms and mites off when the humidity rises. Even with improved seed, I do not trust the pests to stay away on their own.

If the weather is fair and no late frost hits the seedlings, I expect to harvest around 280 kg of seed cotton per mu. That should give me roughly 1,260 kg off the whole plot, enough to cover our living costs and set a little aside.
